CruiseMapper currently has no ship schedule for Port Agilkia Island (Philae Temple, Egypt)

Agilkia Island (aka Agilika Island) is a Nile River cruise port destination located inside the Old Aswan Dam (along the river) and is the site of the Ancient Egyptian Philae temple complex. In 1902, the entire temple complex on Philae Island (downstream of Lake Nasser) was dismantled and relocated to Agilkia due to the flooding of this area to form the reservoir of the Aswan High Dam (1960-70).

A total of 22 Ancient Egyption monuments and architectural sites were threatened by the flooding from Lake Nasser. To preserve them was launched the UNESCO Nubia Campaign. By this grandious project were moved the Abu Simbel temples, Philae temples (Philae Island), Kalabsha temples and the Amada Temple (Nubia's oldest). Also dismantled and relocated were Debod Temple (15 km south of Aswan, moved to Madrid Spain), Dendur Temple (given to NYC's Metropolitan Museum of Art), Taffeh Temple (given to Leiden Holland's Rijksmuseum van Oudheden) and Ellesyia Temple (near Qasr Ibrim, given to Turin Italy's Museo Egizio).

 

Agilkia Island is the present-day site of the Philae temple complex near Aswan. For cruise passengers, this is not a conventional walk-off port: the island is reached only by small motorboat, normally after a road transfer from a Nile cruise mooring in Aswan to the Philae/Shellal Marina. The Temple of Isis is the main reason to visit, and the combination of road transfer, boat ride and archaeological site makes it best treated as a half-day shore visit.

At a Glance

  • Independent sightseeing: Independent with some planning or transport.
  • Access: Boat only; there is no bridge or walk-on access to Agilkia Island.
  • Typical transfer: From central Aswan or many Nile cruise moorings, the Philae boat landing is roughly 8–12 km (5.0–7.5 mi) away, depending on the ship's mooring, usually around 20–30 minutes by road.
  • Boat crossing: Approximately 5–10 minutes each way by local motorboat.
  • Time to allow: About 3–4 hours from Aswan for a comfortable Philae-only visit, including transfers.
  • Terrain: Mostly stone paving with uneven surfaces, steps and exposed areas with limited shade.

Getting from the Cruise Port

Most Nile cruise vessels do not berth at Agilkia itself. They normally call at Aswan, from where passengers travel by coach, private vehicle or taxi to the visitor marina near Shellal and the Aswan Low Dam. Small motorboats then carry visitors across the reservoir to the island's visitor jetty.

Independent travel is possible, but it requires coordinating both the road transfer and the return boat. If arranging the boat yourself, confirm the return arrangement before leaving the marina. For cruise passengers on a tight schedule, a pre-arranged driver or organized excursion removes most of this uncertainty.

Best Ways to Spend Your Time

Philae Temple Complex

Allow about 1.5–2 hours on the island, or 3–4 hours including transfers from Aswan. This is the essential Agilkia visit. The principal monument is the Temple of Isis, surrounded by courtyards, pylons, smaller shrines and waterfront structures. Important highlights include the First Pylon, the birth house or Mammisi, the inner temple chambers, the Temple of Hathor and Trajan's Kiosk.

The visit is practical independently if transport is arranged in advance. A guide is useful for interpreting the reliefs and temple layout, but the complex is compact enough to explore without one.

Philae and the Aswan High Dam

Allow roughly 3.5–4.5 hours. Visitors with a vehicle can combine Philae with the Aswan High Dam. This works well because both lie south of central Aswan, reducing unnecessary backtracking. The dam visit itself is relatively short, so most of the time can still be spent at Philae.

Independent with planning. A hired driver can make this straightforward, although an organized excursion is convenient if the cruise schedule is tight.

Philae, the Unfinished Obelisk and Central Aswan

Allow approximately 5–6 hours. A longer call can include Philae followed by the Unfinished Obelisk and then a return to central Aswan for the Nile waterfront, Nubian Museum or a short walk around the city.

This combination requires road transport between sites. Trying to add several further attractions can make the day rushed, particularly when boat queues and road traffic are taken into account.

Evening Sound and Light Visit

The Philae Sound and Light presentation can be an option for cruises staying in Aswan into the evening or overnight. Because daytime archaeological opening and evening-show arrangements are separate, this is generally more practical as an organized transfer than as a spontaneous independent visit.

Self-Guided Walk on Agilkia Island

Temple of Isis and Waterfront Circuit

Distance: approximately 1–1.5 km (0.6–0.9 mi), depending on detours inside the temple.

Pure walking time: about 20–30 minutes.

Recommended total time: 1.5–2 hours.

Difficulty: Easy to moderate. Distances are short, but expect uneven stone paving, occasional steps and substantial heat exposure.

  1. Visitor jetty: Start where the motorboat drops passengers on Agilkia and follow the main approach toward the temple complex.
  2. Outer courtyard and First Pylon: Enter through the monumental approach and spend time examining the large carved reliefs.
  3. Mammisi: Visit the birth house beside the main temple route before continuing farther into the sanctuary complex.
  4. Temple of Isis: Continue through the courts, columned spaces and inner chambers toward the sanctuary.
  5. Temple of Hathor: After leaving the principal temple, follow the paths toward this smaller structure on the eastern side of the complex.
  6. Trajan's Kiosk: Finish at the distinctive columned pavilion near the water, one of the best viewpoints on the island.
  7. Return to the jetty: Follow the waterfront path back to the boat landing and allow time to locate your assigned or arranged return boat.

The route is short enough for most visitors, but the exposed stone surfaces can become very hot. Allow more time than the distance suggests, especially if stopping frequently for reliefs and interior chambers.

When an Organized Excursion Makes Sense

An organized tour is recommended if the ship has a short Aswan call, if Philae is being combined with several other sites, or if you prefer not to coordinate taxis and local boats independently. Guided tours also add useful context because many of Philae's most interesting features are in the temple reliefs rather than simply in the architecture.

Independent visitors with a longer port call can comfortably arrange a driver to the marina, take the local boat to Agilkia and tour the island on foot.

Practical Tips

  • There is no practical walking route from an Aswan cruise mooring to Agilkia Island; road transport and a boat are required.
  • Confirm how and when your return boat will collect you before beginning the temple visit.
  • Carry sun protection and drinking water. Much of the archaeological complex is exposed, and temperatures in Upper Egypt can be severe.
  • Wear footwear suitable for stone paving, steps and uneven archaeological surfaces.
  • If returning independently to a ship in Aswan, allow a substantial margin for the boat crossing, possible queues, road traffic and reaching the correct cruise mooring. A margin of at least 60–90 minutes after leaving the island is sensible for a time-critical return.
  • For a short call, prioritize Philae rather than attempting to combine it with too many Aswan attractions.
